A keyframe is cut only on a real action, a mark or a visual change. Speech pauses over a static screen never cut extra keyframes. Each row is one trigger, with the

props.title: What cuts a keyframe

text.insert: A spoken cue is the one speech trigger, and it needs measured word times. A Hex transcript never gives cues, because its times are
snap to a transition that starts from 0.3 s before to 1.2 s after the word.
Without such a transition, the cue takes the frame 150 ms after the word.
A cue keyframe is dropped unless its image differs from every keyframe already chosen, by a scene diff of 0.03 or more.
So speech over an unchanged screen still yields one frame.
They are weak because they are usually filler.

allows 6 keyframes below 40 s, one more for each 20 s after that, and at most 12 from 2:20. Each image costs a reading model about 1,000 to 1,500 tokens. Ordinary events fill only the first 6, and the rest go to marks and coverage.
Marks are never dropped, and marks drawn on one screen share one keyframe.
A shared keyframe sits at the last mark of its group and draws the ink of all of them.
The screen counts as the same while the luma grid around the ink, padded by 8%, changed in under 5% of its cells.
A group closes at a click or a drag, past 20 s, or past 12 strokes.
Groups beyond the budget merge with a neighbour: same-screen pairs with the least ink first, else the most alike screens.
Flags stay on their own, and no other keyframe cuts into the span of a group with more than one mark.
Auto-crop gives a group's ink to its own keyframe's crop alone (

After the marks, a stretch longer than 100 words or 35 s gets a frame from inside it when one qualifies. A click, a laser point, a settled scene change or a novel cue qualifies. The lead-in before the first keyframe is its own stretch.

Each keyframe owns the words from the start of the clause in progress at its anchor until the next keyframe's start. The anchor is the action start, the transition start or the cue word. A clause breaks at clause punctuation, at a recognizer segment start, or at a pause of 1.5 s or more. Words before the first keyframe belong to it.
groups strokes into marks and names each shape from the path, measured in pixels. A pause over 1.2 s, or a 7th stroke, starts a new mark. Each row is one shape the test gives:

rows: Ends near its start, is longer than twice its box's long side, fills a third of its box, and its box's short side is over 0.42 of the long side
Is up to 5:1, closes well within its short side and goes round at most about three times, such as a loop round a line of text
Is straight
Is a line with one or two short strokes near one end, or one stroke whose straight shaft turns back at the tip into one or two straight barbs
Is anything else: a hooked underline, ticks, V shapes, zigzags, scribbles and C-shaped arcs

A Screen capture crops each keyframe to where the user was gesturing, so the user records the whole screen instead of picking an area first. Area and Window captures are not cropped.

Between those, a snapshot comes at most every 500 ms while the cursor moves, else every 2 s.
A snapshot is stored only when the list changed, and each one costs about 0.5 ms.

steps.text: Crop a Screen Capture
For Each Keyframe
Take the slice of the timeline halfway to each neighbouring keyframe

A cursor that wanders far from the ink is ignored
If one or two windows hold the activity, crop to those windows
Two windows fit an arrow from one to the other
The crop keeps a menu the window opened and the touched part of the menu bar
If that window is most of the screen, crop to the activity inside it with some context
Edges move into nearby white space and past the ends of the text lines they cross, up to the window's edge
If the keyframe has only talk, keep the previous crop
Merge Neighbours
Merge neighbouring crops that mostly overlap
The sheet does not jitter
If a crop covers most of the screen, keep the whole keyframe

The defaults were tuned on 12 simulated captures with hand-labelled ideal crops. They are a maximized terminal, two windows side by side, an arrow between windows, a tiny badge in a huge window, a menu-bar menu and talk-only keyframes. The rest are a dragged window, overlapping windows, 30 s across three windows, a stray cursor, a full-screen app and a scrolling page.

Each point is measured from five seeds, and
The point and the four pixels 0.5 pt from it, at least 1 px left, right, up and down, are each measured on their own.
Boxes within 1 px of each other on every side count as one answer.
The point's box stands when two of the four give it too, or all four when the point stepped off a mark. When three of the four agree and none gives the point's box, the box is theirs.
Five searches take 0.16 s on a 2560×1440 movie frame, and 0.27 s when the box is most of the frame.
is left out when there is no box, and
when px per pt is known.

A point finds its box the way a region does, from the pixels off one background color that are joined to the point. So the two modes agree within 1 px on the fixtures, on a PNG and on a movie frame. The search runs this path:

steps.text: Find the Box Under a Point
Choose the Window
Search 15 pt round the point first, which finds a small part whatever a movie did to its shades
Else flood-fill from the point within 10 per channel of the mean color under it, and add 3 pt to that box
The fill runs again round its own most common color when the point's color is more than 3 per channel off it
Start from an open place of the fill within 12 pt of the point, with the fill 1.5 pt round it, else half that, else 1 px
Find the Background
Take the main colors on the window's border, most common first, each the mean of its shades
Skip a color that holds under 1/8 of the border or is the point's own
Take the first color that closes a part inside the window or at the image edge
Join the Part
Join pixels that are clearly off the background, by half the point's contrast and 8 to 24 per channel, and whose 8 neighbours are too
Take in the pixels next to those
A part too thin for that, such as a glyph or a line, joins through its clear pixels
Judge the Part
If a small part under 12 pt is a solid shape of its own, keep it as the box
A solid shape is 2.5 pt or more on a side and fills 0.65 of its box
It has no clear pixels within 1.5 pt on its rows, and under 12 pt on both sides it is at most 2:1
If the part is a mark, step to the surface next to it, at most three times
A mark is a glyph, a word, an icon outline, a text line under 20 pt, or a run of the point's color at most 1.5 pt long
If the fill is a pocket, a tinted patch or a sliver, step to the nearest surface of its color
If the part's main color is further off the background than the seed, find the part again at that color's threshold
Report the Box
If no color closes the part, give the flood fill's box, with up to 2 px of blurred edge on each side
Else give the part's box, trimmed as a region trims it
If no surface is found, give no box and say the point is on text or a thin line

text.insert: This is measured, not proven. On a grid of 405 points over a 17 pt label, every point gives the button at 2 px per pt from a PNG, libx264 and VideoToolbox. At 1 px per pt a PNG gives the button everywhere, and each encoder leaves a few points with another box and an unsure note. The test holds each encoded frame to 401 of 405.
takes the most common color on the region's border as the background, and boxes the parts that are off it.
Pixels more than 8 per channel off the background form 8-connected parts, and parts on one row at most 1.5 pt apart join, so a word is one box.
A group of pixels under 6 pt on both sides, none more than 16 per channel off the background, is dropped first as a movie speck.
Each box gives up to 3 px per side whose pixels lean to the background. In a box under 12 pt on both sides, and in every point box, an edge line with 2 pixels that do not lean stays.
A box with a border on a page of another color comes with its border in both modes. A point adds the size of the fill alone, and on a page of the box's own color it gives the fill inside the border.
Parts inside another part's box, parts under 6 pt on either side, and all but the 30 largest are dropped. Past 30, the output says how many smaller boxes it left out.

Each shown box's nearest neighbour that overlaps it on the other axis gives one horizontal or vertical gap. A gap is given only when that neighbour is a shown box, so a gap never spans a box left out.
A part is tested for being inside another only against the parts over its own 64 px cell, so 50,000 parts take under 0.1 s.

text.insert: Px per pt is the full-frame width of the measured image in px over the capture's width in pt. A cropped image counts at its full width. The capture's width is
on the Mac and the device's

, which is every cabled capture, prints px only. Its size limits still need px per pt, so they take an estimate from the frame's shape. A frame 16:9 or taller is an iPhone's, and it gets its short side over 400, rounded. A wider frame is an iPad's, and it gets its short side over 834, never under 1.
The output then says the size limits used an estimate, and
. The estimate sets the limits only, never a size in pt. Positions are full-frame, in pt rounded to 0.5 and in whole px of the recording's pixels.
